contradiction. use an idiosyncratic word — load-bearing, the hinge, non-negotiable. drop a fragment after three full sentences. cite a real source by name. admit you don't know something. add a describing how you write. make claude derive it from what you've already written. most people try to explain their voice to claude in a sentence or two. "write it casual but professional." that produces nothing, because you're describing a feeling and claude needs patterns — how long your sentences run, how you open, how you sign off, the words you reach for and the ones you never touch. you already have thousands of samples of your own writing. point claude at them. the voice profile prompt connect gmail (or outlook), then run this once: read my last 30 sent emails in gmail. write my voice profile: how i greet, how i sign off, my sentence length, my go-to phrases, the words i never use. format it as writing instructions to follow when drafting as me. thirty is roughly the floor. below that claude picks up noise instead of pattern. sent mail beats anything else you could feed it, because it's writing you actually shipped to a real person under a real deadline, rather than writing you polished for an audience. read it before you save it the profile comes back as a list of observations, and this is the part people skip. read it. some of what it finds will be habits you don't want reinforced — i had a stretch of over-apologizing in email that claude dutifully wrote down as a signature move. delete those lines. what's left is your voice, minus the tics. save it where claude will actually read it a voice profile sitting in a chat window is worth nothing next week. put it in the file claude loads at the start of every session — the next section covers exactly where that lives and what else belongs in it. other sources worth feeding it sent email is the best single source, but not the only one. slack messages to your team catch how you write when you're moving fast. your last twenty linkedin posts catch your public register, which is usually different. if you write in two distinct modes — internal versus external — build two profiles and tell claude which one to use. already using this in a workflow the meeting follow-up engine in claude in action runs this same voice profile against meeting transcripts to draft recap emails that sound like you wrote them. build the profile here once, and that workflow gets better for free. 6 step 6 your writing rules file set it once so you stop re-typing the rules in every session. everything above is worthless if you have to remember it each time. the point of a rules file is that claude reads it before it writes a word, every session, without you asking. where it goes cowork: a claude.md file at the root of your project folder. loaded automatically at the start of every session in that folder. claude projects (web or mobile): paste it into the project's custom instructions. neither of those: keep it in a note and paste it at the top of any session where the writing matters. the starter block copy this whole thing. swap in your own voice profile from step 5 where marked. ## writing rules apply these to every draft you write for me. **banned words.** delve, leverage, utilize, facilitate, robust, seamless, paramount, multifaceted, holistic, ever-evolving, pivotal, crucial, furthermore, moreover, additionally **banned phrases.** "in today's fast-paced world," "it's important to note," "that said," "at its core," "when it comes to," "navigate the landscape," "paradigm shift," "game-changer," "by doing x you can y," "in conclusion" **four laws.** 1. specificity over generality. a number, name, or date in every paragraph. 2. vary rhythm. never three same-length sentences in a row. 3. make claims. take sides. name names. 4. cut connectors. use a period instead. **structure.** no "key takeaways" section. no heading every 80 words. no three-item lists by default. one em-dash per 125 words, maximum. **my voice.** [paste your voice profile from step 5 here] never tell me a draft is done. tell me what you'd cut next. the one-off version for a session where you don't want to set anything up, this does most of the work on its own: write [task]. hard rules: - no banned words: leverage, delve, robust, utilize, facilitate, seamless, paramount, holistic, pivotal, crucial - cut every "however," "furthermore," "moreover," "additionally" and use a period - vary sentence length wildly: at least two under 8 words, at least one over 25 - every paragraph needs a specific number, name, or date - no three-item lists. no "it's not just x, it's y." no rhetorical questions that you answer in the next sentence. - sound like a tired senior operator texting, not a brand voice. the line that does the most work "sound like a tired senior operator texting, not a brand voice." one sentence, and it fixes more than the whole banned list — because it's a target rather than a prohibition. claude is better at writing toward something than at avoiding things. 7 step 7 the sniff tests twelve checks on a finished draft. none takes more than a minute. run these on anything going out under your name. most drafts fail two or three, and fixing those two or three is usually the whole job. test how to run it em-dash count per 500 words. ai averages 4–9, people average 1–3. over 5 means half need to become commas or periods. hedge count count "it's important to note," "however," "arguably," "could," "may," "in many cases" per 500 words. three or more is the ai hedge pattern. subject-first ratio how many sentences open with "the," "this," "it," or "our"? ai runs 60%+. people run 30–40%. reorder until you're under 50%. paragraph variance all paragraphs three or four sentences? that's the ai default. people cluster 1, 2, 5, 1, 7. connector density "furthermore," "moreover," "additionally," "in conclusion." one or more per paragraph reads as ai. adverb density words ending in -ly. ai runs 2–3 per paragraph. target 0–1. cut "significantly," "ultimately," "essentially," "basically" first. passive ratio "is / was / been / are" plus a past participle. ai runs 20–30%. target under 10%. three-item count count the "a, b, and c" lists. convert at least one to a pair, or split it into separate sentences. vague-noun audit "area," "space," "landscape," "realm," "domain," "opportunity" with nothing specific attached. each one needs a name, a number, or an example. claim-to-evidence ratio every claim should have evidence next to it — a number, a name, an anecdote. ai drifts to three claims per piece of evidence. the slack test paste a paragraph into slack to a colleague. would they reply "...what?" if so, it's too formal. the reorder test shuffle three paragraphs. if the new order reads as well as the old one, the prose has no rhythm. have claude grade its own draft score this draft against the twelve sniff tests in my writing rules. for each test, give the actual count and pass or fail. then rewrite only the sentences that caused the failures. don't touch anything that passed. the read-aloud test beats all twelve read the draft out loud at speaking pace. mark every sentence that trips you, sounds canned, or you'd never say to a person. rewrite those. it catches things no counting exercise will, and it takes about as long as the piece takes to read. 8 step 8 the cheat sheet one screen. everything on this page, compressed. if you read nothing else here, read this. the nine-pass edit, in order don't try to fix a draft in one pass. cut before you add, structure before you polish. pass what you're hunting 1. hedge cut every weakening qualifier. if the sentence becomes a confident claim without it, the cut was right. 2. banned-word swap run the swap list. if there's no clean replacement, cut the sentence. 3. connector cull delete 60% of the "howevers" and "furthermores." replace with a period. 4. opening variation read the first three words of every sentence. three in a row starting the same way? rewrite one. 5. length burst add at least two sentences under 8 words and one over 28. 6. specificity injection every vague noun and metric-free claim gets a name, number, or date. 7. claim density every paragraph needs one arguable claim. pure-background paragraphs get folded in or killed. 8. voice injection one human signal per 200 words. a fragment, a contradiction, a specific story. 9. read aloud rewrite everything that trips. the four rules worth memorizing put a number, name, or date in every paragraph. never write three same-length sentences in a row. make a claim someone could argue with. cut the connector. use a period. the prompt that does the most in one line rewrite this so the final version is 30% shorter and 100% more specific. every sentence you cut was either hedging, repeating a claim, or adding no fact. sound like a tired senior operator texting, not a brand voice. the takeaway none of this makes claude write for you. it makes claude stop writing like claude, which is a different and more useful thing. the specifics still have to come from you — the number, the name, the thing that actually happened. claude can't invent those, and every tell on this page is really just claude covering for the fact that it doesn't have them. next step build your voice profile from step 5, paste it into the rules file in step 6, and run your next real draft through the sniff tests in step 7. that's about twenty minutes, and it's the last time you'll have to think about any of this. ← previous claude in office all guides next → claude everywhere claude writing by steve gustafson. how to stop claude text: 1 step 1 what is claude cowork? think of it as hiring an ai assistant who sits at a desk next to you. most people know claude as a chatbot: you type a question, you get an answer. cowork is different. instead of answering one question at a time, claude takes on actual work: writing documents, building spreadsheets, researching companies, making presentations, analyzing data, all as real files on your computer. regular claude (chat) claude cowork you ask, claude answers you assign a task, claude does the work text responses only creates real files: word, excel, powerpoint, pdf no access to your files reads and writes to a folder on your computer forgets between sessions remembers your context the bottom line cowork turns claude from a chatbot into a co-worker. you describe what you need, claude figures out the steps and executes them, and you get a real deliverable you can use immediately. what people hand to cowork daily documents & writing memos, proposals, reports, emails, and posts as polished word docs or pdfs. research deep-dive a company, person, or topic and get a sourced research document. presentations real powerpoint decks you can open in powerpoint or google slides. spreadsheets & data excel files with formulas and charts. analyze a csv. build a dashboard. one thing to know up front: why your usage limit disappears every message you send makes claude re-read the whole conversation from the top. message 1 is cheap. message 30 means claude re-reads 29 exchanges before it even starts on your new request. that is why long chats burn your limit fast. every "start fresh" tip later in this guide traces back to this one fact.

text: 2 step 2 get set up in 5 minutes download, sign in, pick a folder. one choice matters more than the rest. before you start • a mac (apple silicon m1 or newer) or windows pc (x64) • a paid claude plan: pro ($20/month) , max, team, or enterprise. cowork is not on the free plan. 2.1 download and sign in get the desktop app at claude.com/download , install it, and sign in with your anthropic account. then look at the top of the window: you'll see chat , cowork , and code tabs. click cowork . (ignore code, that's for software developers.) heads up: the first time you open cowork it downloads a ~2gb environment. this happens once and can take 5-10 minutes. let it finish. 2.2 pick a folder, and put it in your cloud drive cowork asks you to choose a folder. this is the one setup choice worth thirty seconds, because moving it later is a chore: create the folder inside your cloud-synced drive, not a plain local folder. something like google drive/cowork os . use whatever your work already runs on: google drive, dropbox, onedrive/sharepoint, or box. claude can only see files inside this folder, not your whole computer. why the cloud drive, specifically your mac still treats it as an ordinary local folder, so nothing about daily cowork changes. but the same files now sit in a service claude has a connector for, and that is what lets cowork on your phone or the web reach your work at all. a plain local folder is desktop-only forever. so is icloud, which syncs between your own devices but has no claude connector. google drive, dropbox, onedrive/sharepoint, and box all have connectors. full rule in claude everywhere . one setting to change in google drive google drive for desktop streams files by default, meaning they're online-only placeholders until opened, and cowork can fail to read them. right-click your cowork folder in finder and choose available offline (or switch drive to mirror mode) so the files are genuinely local. dropbox calls it "make available offline." how a session works type a request in plain english and be specific: "write a one-page executive summary of my company for investors. make it a word doc." claude asks a clarifying question or two if it needs to, works through the task while you watch or switch apps, then hands you a link to the finished file already sitting in your folder. no downloading. you don't have to wait while claude works, keep typing. your messages queue and claude picks them up as it finishes each step, so you can add context or stack up follow-on tasks. it's like leaving notes on a colleague's desk while they're heads-down. just keep the app running while a task is going, minimizing is fine, quitting is not.

title: Organize With Projects
desc: Cowork's built-in way to keep work separated, with memory that persists.
text: 4 step 4 organize with projects cowork's built-in way to keep work separated, with memory that persists. once you're doing more than one-off tasks, use projects , cowork's first-party feature (built in since march 2026). a project is a persistent workspace with its own files, instructions, and memory. everything inside stays scoped to that project, so claude remembers your context across tasks without you re-explaining anything. create one in four steps 4.1 open the projects panel in claude desktop, click projects in the left sidebar, then new project . 4.2 name it and add instructions give it a clear name ("wuunderfund", "q2 marketing"). in the instructions field, add a few lines on how claude should work here: tone, formatting, key context. these apply to every task in the project. 4.3 attach context add a local folder , link a chat project , or paste a url for claude to reference. this is what claude draws from when it works. 4.4 start a task type your request. claude now has your instructions and context loaded automatically. memory is automatic here as you work, claude saves useful facts, decisions, and preferences on its own (roughly every 5,000 tokens), and loads them at the start of your next task in that project. memory stays scoped: what claude learns in project a never shows up in project b. want to force something in? say "remember this." want to see it? open the memory icon in the project view. that's enough to run on a project with a folder attached and three lines of instructions is a complete setup for most people. the next step is optional: a plugin that scaffolds a fuller workspace for you in one command. skip it and keep working, or set it up when you want more structure.

label: Claude Beginner · Step 5 · Optional
title: Power Up in One Command
desc: A free plugin builds a full workspace for you, so you never set one up by hand.
headings: Get CoWork OS and Install It
Open a new session and type /begin
text: 5 step 5 · optional power up in one command a free plugin builds a full workspace for you, so you never set one up by hand. projects handle the basics. if you want a fuller system, an identity file that spans every project, reusable templates, a clean split between what claude reads and what it writes, explicit memory you control, you have two options: build it by hand, or let a plugin do it in one command. start with the plugin. install once, type /begin , done cowork os is a free plugin (by paul j lipsky) that sets up your whole workspace through a short conversation. install it, open a new session, type /begin , and answer a few questions. about five minutes later you have folders, an identity file, workspace rules, and a memory system, all built for you. get cowork os and install it download the plugin, then point cowork at it. about two minutes. 📦 cowork-os-plugin.zip download the plugin by paul j lipsky. we host a copy here so the link never breaks. 1 download and unzip unzip the file. you get a folder called cowork-os-plugin . put it anywhere you can find again. 2 install from folder in cowork, click customize (top-right), then browse plugins , then install from folder . choose the cowork-os-plugin folder you just unzipped. 3 open a new session and type /begin the plugin registers its commands. type /begin and answer the questions. if /begin does not appear, restart the cowork session. installing other plugins the plugins elsewhere on this site come as a single .plugin file instead of a folder. for those: download the file, then drag it into a cowork session or double-click it, and click install. if a plugin lives in a github repo, add it with /plugin marketplace add [user]/[repo] , then /plugin install [name] . since august 2026 you can also point the marketplace at the web address of a plugin zip. what /begin asks, and builds claude asks you… what it builds your name and role? an identity file so claude knows who you are on every task your company, and what you do day to day? context so claude understands your world what tools do you use? so claude knows which formats to create how do you like to work? behavior rules: direct vs detailed, short vs thorough any projects you're on right now? a folder with isolated memory for each one when it finishes, your cloud folder holds an identity file, a templates folder, per-project folders, a place for everything claude creates, workspace rules, and a memory file, all filled in from your answers. from then on, "remember this: [fact]" saves a note that persists, and "new project: [name]" spins up an isolated folder and memory in one line. want to understand or build it by hand? you don't need to, the plugin handles it. but if you want to know exactly what each piece does, or set it up manually and tune it, that's power-user territory. the advanced guide covers the folder architecture, the identity file, and the claude.md + memory.md system in full.

label: Claude Beginner · Step 6
title: Connect Your Tools & Pick a Model
desc: Give Claude access to your apps, and know which model to reach for.
text: 6 step 6 connect your tools & pick a model give claude access to your apps, and know which model to reach for. optional, but powerful connectors and plugins aren't required. but they turn claude from a general assistant into a specialist that pulls data from your tools and does domain work at a professional level. most people add two or three in their first week. connectors: plug in your apps a connector gives claude direct access to a tool, no copy-pasting, no exporting. adding one takes about 30 seconds: click "connect" and sign in. there are 50+ across every category. the ones most people start with: connector what claude can do google drive read and reference your docs, sheets, and slides gmail read, draft, and send email; search your inbox google calendar read your schedule, find conflicts, prep for meetings slack read channels, search messages, catch up on what you missed hubspot / salesforce pull crm contacts, deals, and account records full directory at claude.com/connectors . all free. add one via cowork → customize → connectors. install claude in chrome first one browser extension lets claude see and act in your browser: fill forms, pull data from a live page, take screenshots. combined with cowork, you can say "look at this page and write a competitive analysis" and claude reads the page, then creates the word doc. search "claude" in the chrome web store . beyond connectors, plugins teach claude to do role-specific work (sales, marketing, finance, legal, data, and more), each bundling skills and templates built by anthropic. browse them under customize, and see the advanced guide for building your own. which model should you use? claude comes in four models. you pick yours in the cowork interface. from fastest to most capable: haiku 4.5 , the fastest and cheapest. reach for it on quick, simple jobs: reformatting text, a one-line question, high-volume back-and-forth. sonnet 5 , the everyday default. fast, and close to opus-level on real work. it handles most of what you'll throw at it. start here. opus 5 , the deep-work model and the cost-effective pick for hard tasks. best when the work needs careful reasoning or runs long, and it clears the large majority of demanding work for less than fable 5. make it your default when a job is genuinely hard. fable 5 , the most capable model anthropic ships. built for the hardest reasoning and long-horizon work. it costs more per token than opus, so save it for the roughly 10% of tasks where opus gets stuck. rule of thumb: start with sonnet 5. move up to opus 5 when the task is high-stakes, complex, or long-running. drop to haiku 4.5 for something quick. escalate to fable 5 only when opus can't crack it.

label: Claude Advanced · Section 1
title: Build Your Own Skills
desc: Turn your repeated instructions into reusable, auto-triggering capabilities.
headings: You should build a skill when:
You don't need a skill when:
text: 1 section 1 build your own skills turn your repeated instructions into reusable, auto-triggering capabilities. if you followed the level 1 guide, you've already been using skills without knowing it. when you say "new project" and claude creates folders, memory files, and output directories, that's a skill in action. the "new project" workflow, the file naming conventions, the per-project memory, all of these are patterns that could be (and are) encoded as skills. now you'll learn to build your own. a skill is a markdown file called skill.md that teaches claude a specific capability. every time you find yourself giving claude the same instructions, "format reports this way," "research companies using this framework," "always check these 5 things", that's a skill waiting to be built. when to build a skill you should build a skill when: you give the same instructions 3+ times. you have a specific workflow or framework. you want consistent output quality across sessions. you want to share a process with colleagues. you don't need a skill when: it's a one-time task. the instructions are simple enough to type each time. the process changes frequently and isn't standardized yet. skill file structure my-skill/ skill.md ← required: instructions + metadata template.md ← optional: reference files examples/ ← optional: example inputs/outputs skill.md anatomy every skill has two parts: yaml frontmatter (metadata) and markdown body (instructions). --- name: company-research description: deep competitive intelligence research on any company, delivered as a professional word document. use when the user says 'research [company]', 'competitive profile', 'company deep dive'. --- ## instructions when the user asks you to research a company: 1. search the web for the company's website, recent news, funding, and key people 2. analyze their product, pricing, go-to-market strategy 3. identify 3-5 direct competitors 4. deliver as a formatted .docx with sections: - company overview - product & positioning - business model - competitive landscape - key risks & opportunities the description is everything claude decides whether to auto-invoke a skill based entirely on the description field. be specific about trigger phrases. vague descriptions = skills that never fire. include examples of what users might say: "research [company]", "tell me about [company]", "competitive profile". where skills live location scope priority ~/.claude/skills/ all your projects (personal) high .claude/skills/ in project that project only medium inside a plugin anyone who installs the plugin standard enterprise managed entire organization highest the easy way: use /skill-creator if you have the cowork os plugin installed, type /skill-creator in any session. claude will interview you about what you want the skill to do, write the skill.md for you, test it, and optimize the description for reliable triggering. you don't need to write yaml by hand. advanced: dynamic context injection skills can pull live data using shell commands: !`git log --oneline -5` injects your recent commits. !`cat package.json | jq .dependencies` injects your project dependencies. this happens before claude sees the skill, so the data is always fresh.

label: Claude Advanced · Section 2
title: Create & Distribute Plugins
desc: Bundle your skills, connectors, and commands into shareable packages.
text: 2 section 2 create & distribute plugins bundle your skills, connectors, and commands into shareable packages. a plugin is a folder that bundles skills, commands, and connector configurations into a single installable package. if skills are individual tools, plugins are the toolbox. plugin folder structure my-plugin/ .claude-plugin/ plugin.json ← required: name, version, author skills/ company-research/ skill.md person-research/ skill.md commands/ research.md ← slash commands: /research .mcp.json ← optional: mcp tool connections plugin.json (the minimum) { "name": "my-research-toolkit", "version": "1.0.0", "description": "company and person research with word doc output", "author": "your name" } critical: don't put skills inside .claude-plugin/ only plugin.json goes inside the .claude-plugin/ directory. skills, commands, and agents go at the plugin root level. this is the most common mistake when building plugins. distribution methods 1. github (recommended) push your plugin folder to a github repo. anyone installs with: /plugin marketplace add your-username/your-repo . free, versioned, and easy to update. 2. direct file sharing zip the plugin folder as a .plugin file and email or share it. recipients drop it into their cowork plugins folder. 3. official anthropic marketplace submit through anthropic's review process for broad distribution. must pass security and quality standards.

label: Claude Advanced · Section 3
title: Share Skills With Your Network
desc: Your best workflows shouldn't die on your laptop.
text: 3 section 3 share skills with your network your best workflows shouldn't die on your laptop. once you've built skills or plugins that work well, sharing them is straightforward. sharing a single skill zip the skill folder (the one containing skill.md) as a .skill file. send it to anyone. they drop it into their ~/.claude/skills/ directory. done. sharing a plugin (via github) 1. create a public github repo 2. push your plugin folder (with .claude-plugin/plugin.json at root) 3. share the install command: /plugin marketplace add your-username/your-repo 4. recipients run that command in cowork. installed instantly. community ecosystem the claude skills community is growing fast. here are places to find and share skills: anthropics/knowledge-work-plugins official anthropic plugins repo on github. sales, finance, legal, marketing, product, data, design, operations plugins with full source code. great reference for building your own. travisvn/awesome-claude-skills community-curated list of 37+ skills and growing. covers coding, research, writing, and workflow automation. fork it, add yours, submit a pr. pro move: create a team plugin if your team repeatedly does the same workflows, build a plugin that encodes your processes. new team members install it on day one and immediately have your best practices available. no training deck needed, the skill is the training.

label: Claude Advanced · Section 4
title: Chrome Extension Power Moves
desc: Turn your browser into an autonomous agent.
text: 4 section 4 chrome extension power moves turn your browser into an autonomous agent. on august 12, 2026, claude in chrome stopped being a separate extension. the side panel is now a full cowork session, the same one you run on desktop, web, and mobile. your skills and connectors work inside it, which they did not before. start a task in chrome, finish it on your desktop, the context carries over. claude still sees, clicks, types, and navigates any page. it does that as cowork now, not as a bolt-on tool. what you can actually do multi-tab orchestration claude manages multiple tabs simultaneously. drag tabs into claude's group, and it can read and act across all of them. "compare pricing across these 5 competitor websites." form filling & data entry claude fills forms using context it already has. "fill out this vendor registration form using our company details." works with any web form. web scraping & data extraction "go to linkedin and pull the last 20 posts from these 5 people into a spreadsheet." claude navigates, reads, extracts, and organizes. gif recording record browser interactions as gif animations with click indicators and action labels. perfect for creating demos, tutorials, and documentation. debug & development claude reads console logs, dom state, and network requests directly. "check why the login page is throwing a 403", it reads the actual error. scheduled browser tasks combine cowork in chrome with scheduled tasks. "every morning at 9am, check these 3 dashboards and summarize what changed." requirements & limitations out of beta as of august 2026. works on chrome and edge, not brave or arc. available now on max and team, rolling out to pro. enterprise stays off by default, and admins can limit it to approved domains. claude uses your existing logins, so it can reach anything you are signed into. be deliberate about which tabs sit in the claude group. a newer check reviews consequential actions, form submits, sends, and downloads, against what you first asked before it goes ahead.

label: Claude Advanced · Section 5
title: Computer Use, Desktop Control
desc: Claude controls your mouse and keyboard to operate native apps.
headings: How Claude Decides What to Use
What You Can Do With It
text: 5 section 5 computer use, desktop control claude controls your mouse and keyboard to operate native apps. cowork reaches a service through a connector when that service has one. it drives the page through chrome when the service does not. but what about everything else, finder, notes, maps, system settings, photoshop, excel (the desktop app), or any native application? that's computer use . claude takes screenshots of your screen, moves the mouse, clicks buttons, and types, just like a remote coworker sitting at your desk. how claude decides what to use this is the mental model that makes everything click. when you give claude a task, it picks the fastest, most reliable tool available: the 3-tier decision hierarchy 1. connectors first slack, calendar, gmail, drive → 2. browser second cowork in chrome for web apps → 3. screen control last mouse + keyboard for native apps connectors are fast and precise, they use each service's api. chrome is that same cowork session driving a web page, for apps without a connector. screen control is the fallback for everything else. how to enable it computer use is off by default. to turn it on: settings → desktop app → general → turn on browser use ✓ → turn on computer use ✓ claude always asks permission before touching a new app. you approve each application explicitly, and you can stop it at any time. what you can do with it native app automation "organize my downloads folder, move pdfs to documents, images to photos, delete anything older than 30 days." claude opens finder and does it. cross-app workflows "pull the metrics from this dashboard in chrome, drop them into the excel spreadsheet on my desktop, then email the updated file." three apps, one prompt. fill desktop forms "fill out this insurance application in preview using my info from the about me file." claude reads your context and types into native form fields. system management "check my disk space, clear the trash, and tell me what's taking up the most storage." claude navigates system settings and finder to investigate. steering claude mid-task computer use is live, you can redirect claude while it works. these steering prompts are your remote control: steering prompt what it does "stop. don't click that yet." pauses before a risky action "use chrome, not safari." redirects to a different app "take a screenshot and show me before you send it." review checkpoint before proceeding "skip slack. open the browser instead." overrides the default tool choice "actually, start over. new approach." full reset mid-task the "come back to review" pattern combine computer use with dispatch for fire-and-forget workflows: 1. send a task from your phone (dispatch) 2. add: "text me when it's done." 3. claude works on your desktop while you're away. 4. you review the result on your mac when you're back. this works for any computer use task. export a deck to pdf, attach it to a calendar invite, organize files, all while you're at lunch. limitations & safety mac only (windows coming soon). claude asks permission per app before interacting. browsers are read-only via computer use (use the chrome extension instead for clicking and typing in web apps). terminals and ides allow clicking but not typing (use the built-in bash tool instead). claude won't enter passwords, execute trades, or move money on your behalf.

label: Claude Advanced · Section 6
title: Scheduled Tasks & Recurring Automation
desc: Set it once, it runs forever.
text: 6 section 6 scheduled tasks & recurring automation set it once, it runs forever. cowork can run tasks on a schedule, daily, weekly, or at specific times. combined with plugins and chrome, this is where cowork becomes an autonomous operator. cron syntax (simplified) schedule cron expression plain english every morning 0 9 * * * 9:00 am daily weekdays only 0 9 * * 1-5 9:00 am mon-fri every monday 30 8 * * 1 8:30 am mondays first of month 0 0 1 * * midnight, 1st day real-world examples morning briefing daily at 9am: summarize unread emails, check calendar, create a priorities list with talking points for today's meetings. outputs a markdown file you review with coffee. weekly invoice cleanup fridays at 5pm: scan email for invoices received this week, extract amounts and vendors, add to a tracking spreadsheet, flag anything over $5k for review. competitor monitor every monday: check 5 competitor websites for pricing changes, new features, or blog posts. compile a diff report showing what changed since last week. key limitation your computer must be awake and the claude desktop app must be open for scheduled tasks to run. if your mac is asleep at 9am, the task runs when you open the lid. tasks don't run in the cloud.

label: Claude Advanced · Section 7
title: Memory Architecture Mastery
desc: The 4-layer system that makes Claude feel like a long-term colleague.
text: 7 section 7 memory architecture mastery the 4-layer system that makes claude feel like a long-term colleague. claude's memory isn't one thing, it's a hierarchy. with the march 2026 projects update, there are now four distinct layers . understanding them lets you put the right information in the right place. the 4 layers layer 1: personal preferences (global) where: claude desktop → settings → personal preferences scope: every conversation, every project, every session what goes here: your name, role, communication style, personality preferences, behavioral rules. things that are always true about how you want claude to work. layer 2: native project instructions & memory (built-in) where: project → instructions field + automatic memory.md scope: all tasks within that project what goes here: project-level tone, formatting rules, and key context in the instructions field. auto-memory captures decisions and patterns as you work, claude decides what's worth saving. first 200 lines (or 25kb) load at the start of each new task. layer 3: claude.md (cowork os, structured rules) where: claude.md file in your workspace folder (or subfolder) scope: that specific folder only what goes here: detailed folder protocols, naming conventions, session start behavior, project registry, read-only/write-only rules. more structured and opinionated than native instructions, this is your operating system. layer 4: memory.md (cowork os, explicit memory) where: memory.md in your workspace folder scope: persistent across sessions, user-controlled what goes here: decisions, deadlines, status updates, things you specifically want remembered with your exact wording. say "remember this" to write; "forget that" to delete. unlike auto-memory, nothing gets saved unless you ask. native memory vs. explicit memory this is the most common question: "if projects auto-remember things, why do i need memory.md?" because they serve different purposes: native auto-memory memory.md (cowork os) trigger automatic, claude decides user-triggered, "remember this" content whatever claude thinks is useful exactly what you told it to save structure unstructured, claude-formatted your format, your categories control low, claude curates high, you curate risk may save noise or miss critical facts you might forget to say "remember this" best for background context, patterns, preferences key decisions, deadlines, exact specifications use both let auto-memory catch the patterns you'd forget to save. use memory.md for the facts you need to persist with precision. they're complementary, not competing. auto-memory is your safety net; memory.md is your source of truth. watch for the validation loop persistent memory is powerful, but it comes with a subtle risk. claude saves your preferences, learns your patterns, and adapts to your style over time. that's the point. but it also means claude gets increasingly tuned to tell you what you want to hear. mit researchers have demonstrated that sycophantic ai creates a feedback loop: your belief strengthens because the ai keeps confirming it, not because it's right. the more personalized your setup, the stronger this effect. counterweights: add a pushback rule to your claude.md ( "flag gaps in my reasoning directly" ), periodically ask claude to argue the opposite side, and for high-stakes decisions, open a fresh session and present your conclusion without the backstory. a new session has no history of agreeing with you. the cold-read review your best editor is a copy of claude that has never seen your work. open a new session with no project, paste only the draft or the code, and ask: is this good, and what is weak? because the fresh session has no memory of agreeing with you, it catches what your main thread waves through. use it on anything that matters before it leaves your hands. the 15-20 message rule long conversations are token furnaces. after 15-20 messages, you're spending more tokens re-reading history than generating new output. when a session gets long: ask claude to summarize everything important, copy that summary, open a new session, paste it as your first message. clean slate, full context, fraction of the cost. pro tip: at the end of a session, prompt "write a session-notes.md with the key decisions and next steps." next session, start with "read session-notes.md first." multi-project isolation both native projects and cowork os support project-scoped isolation. each native project has its own auto-memory. each cowork os subfolder can have its own claude.md and memory.md. your marketing project's claude has different context than your finance project's claude. keep claude.md under 200 lines claude reads the entire claude.md at the start of every session. if it's 500+ lines, you're eating context window for instructions instead of actual work. move detailed reference material into separate files that claude can read when needed. split a big claude.md into parts once your claude.md passes a few hundred lines, break it into named files: identity, writing rules, project context. pull them in with an @include line so the main file stays a short table of contents. the deeper habit is separating what from how: keep your reusable instructions in files, keep one-off asks in the chat. when the two blur, both get harder to fix.

label: Claude Advanced · Section 8
title: Set Up the Workspace by Hand
desc: The folder architecture and identity file the /begin plugin builds for you, explained so you can build and tune them yourself.
headings: Fast Track: Import Your Context From ChatGPT
text: 8 section 8 set up the workspace by hand the folder architecture and identity file the /begin plugin builds for you, explained so you can build and tune them yourself. the cowork os plugin scaffolds all of this in one /begin command, and most people should let it. this section is for when you want to understand exactly what it builds, or set it up manually and tune every piece. the memory layer that sits on top, claude.md and memory.md, is covered in memory architecture mastery above; this is the folders and the identity file underneath it. the folder architecture the core idea is one separation: where claude reads from versus where claude writes to . native projects don't enforce this, so without a structure your inputs and outputs pile into one folder. here's the layout power users run, all of it inside the cloud-synced drive you picked during setup: google drive/cowork os/ ← your cloud drive, not a local folder about me/ about-me.md ← who you are, your role, your style templates/ report-template.md ← structures claude should reuse projects/ ← reference materials (claude reads, never writes) my-startup/ pitch-deck.pptx claude outputs/ ← everything claude creates goes here my-startup/ claude.md ← instructions for claude (the brain) memory.md ← persistent notes across sessions about me/ your identity file. claude reads it at the start of every session. this is what makes claude feel like your assistant instead of a generic ai. detailed below. templates/ document structures claude should follow: a report format, an email style, a deck skeleton. claude studies the pattern and applies it without copying the content. start empty; add as you find patterns you reuse. projects/ context claude needs: briefs, research, past work, organized by project. claude reads from here but never writes to it, so your originals stay untouched. claude outputs/ every file claude creates lands here, mirroring your projects folders. keeps the workspace clean and makes deliverables easy to find. you don't build it manually you never have to create these by hand. in a session, say "set up my workspace with an about me folder, templates folder, projects folder, and claude outputs folder," and claude creates them. saying "new project: [name]" then adds a projects/[name]/ and a matching claude outputs/[name]/ with its own project-scoped memory. file naming convention use one pattern for everything claude creates: project_contenttype_v1.ext example what it is acme_proposal_v1.docx first draft of a proposal for acme q2-launch_deck_v2.pptx second revision of the q2 launch deck monthly_report_v3.xlsx third revision of a monthly report ask claude to revise something and it increments the version (v1 → v2 → v3), giving you a built-in history with no git required. install obsidian to actually edit your folder (free, 2 minutes) cowork runs on .md files. double-click one and it opens in textedit as a mess of hashtags and asterisks, so most people quietly stop editing their context, and their setup never gets smarter. fix it with obsidian : free for personal use, runs locally, renders markdown cleanly. download it, choose "open folder as vault" , point it at your cowork folder. now you browse and edit context in obsidian and generate new work in cowork, same files, no syncing. not notion (it corrupts markdown with hidden formatting) and not google docs (constant conversion). obsidian just reads your folder without touching it. keep the workspace lean cowork reads your folder before every task. that's how claude knows you, but don't dump 50 files in "just in case." your about me, claude.md, templates, and active project files are essential. last quarter's 47-page board pdf is not, move it out until you need it. and prune claude outputs/ weekly, or claude starts reading stale drafts as context. the identity file (about me) a plain text file in about me/ that tells claude who you are and how you work. without it, every session starts cold. with it, claude works like a colleague who's known you for months. the structure: # about [your name] ## who i am [your name], [role] at [company]. what you do day to day. ## what i'm working on - [current focus, projects, deadlines] ## tools i use - [google docs, slack, excel, etc.] ## how i like to work - [brief and direct? detailed? response-length preference?] ## things to know - [jargon, acronyms, context that helps claude do better work] keep it under 2,000 words cowork reads this before every single task. if it's a novel, that's thousands of tokens burned before any work starts, every time. trim to what claude needs to do good work for you. think resume, not autobiography. fast track: import your context from chatgpt if you've used chatgpt for months, you've already built up your role, preferences, and corrections. extract it instead of starting from scratch. start the export now, it takes 1-3 days chatgpt's data export isn't instant. go to chatgpt.com → profile icon → settings → data controls → export data → confirm. you'll get an email from noreply@openai.com with a link that expires in 24 hours. check spam. let claude do the extraction unzip the export (you'll get chat.html ), drop it in your workspace, and tell claude: "i just exported my chatgpt history. it's in chat.html. read through it and extract: (1) everything it knew about me, role, company, preferences, (2) instructions i repeated often, (3) recurring projects, (4) key decisions and facts. use what you find to draft my about me and seed my memory.md." what took months to teach chatgpt, claude picks up in one conversation.

label: Claude Advanced · Section 9
title: MCP: Connect Anything
desc: The protocol that lets Claude talk to any tool, database, or API.
headings: Why Build a Custom MCP Connector?
text: 9 section 9 mcp: connect anything the protocol that lets claude talk to any tool, database, or api. mcp (model context protocol) is how claude connects to external services. every connector you use, google drive, slack, gmail, github, is an mcp server under the hood. you can build your own. why build a custom mcp connector? connect internal tools your company's crm, ticketing system, internal wiki, or custom database. if it has an api, claude can connect to it. automate proprietary workflows "pull this week's support tickets from zendesk, categorize them, and create a summary for the team standup." requires a zendesk mcp connector. mcp architecture (simplified) your tool / api ↑ mcp server (your code: translates between claude and your api) ↑ mcp protocol (standardized json messages) ↑ claude desktop (the client that calls your server) two types of mcp servers type where it runs best for desktop your local machine local databases, file systems, local tools remote cloud server (https) web apis, shared team tools, multi-device access start simple before building a custom mcp connector, check if one already exists. cowork's connector directory has 50+ pre-built integrations. type your tool name in the customize → connectors search. if it's there, you're done in 2 clicks. turn off what you're not using web search, connectors, and extended thinking all add tokens to every response, even when you don't need them. writing your own content? turn off search. simple grammar check? skip extended thinking. and when you do use connectors, be specific: "search slack from the last 7 days for messages about the q2 launch" costs way less than "search slack for anything about launches." features are a dial, not a switch.

label: Claude Advanced · Section 10
title: Parallel Agents
desc: Claude doesn't just do one thing at a time. It can split into teams.
headings: The Magic Phrase: "Use parallel agents wherever possible"
text: 10 section 10 parallel agents claude doesn't just do one thing at a time. it can split into teams. when claude encounters a task that can be broken into independent pieces, it automatically spawns sub-agents , parallel workers that execute simultaneously. this is one of the most powerful features most people never discover. how it works say you ask: "research these 8 companies and create a competitive matrix." instead of researching them one by one (slow), claude spawns 8 parallel agents that each research one company simultaneously. results come back in minutes instead of an hour. when to trigger parallel agents the magic phrase: "use parallel agents wherever possible" include this in your request when the task involves multiple independent workstreams. claude will automatically identify what can run in parallel and split the work. you can also include this in your personal preferences or claude.md so claude always looks for parallelization opportunities. great tasks for parallel agents research multiple entities "research these 5 companies", each company gets its own agent researching simultaneously. multi-file analysis "analyze these 10 spreadsheets and summarize findings", each file gets its own agent. content at scale "write social posts for each of these 8 topics", parallel content generation. code across modules "update the frontend, backend, and tests for this feature", three agents working different parts. agent types type what it does best for general-purpose full capabilities: search, read, write, execute most tasks explore read-only: fast search and analysis research, codebase exploration plan decision-focused: architecture and strategy planning before execution token cost each sub-agent has its own context window. running 8 parallel agents uses roughly 8x the tokens of a single agent. this is most effective on opus or sonnet where reasoning quality justifies the cost. don't parallelize trivial tasks. batch tasks, target edits three separate messages = three full context reloads. one message with three tasks = one reload. and when something needs fixing, don't say "redo the report." say "only redo section 3, keep everything else." every full regeneration burns the entire output token count again. point to the specific section. tell claude what's wrong with it. add "no commentary. just the output." when you know exactly what you want. match the model to the task opus + extended thinking is your heavy machinery. don't use it to move a chair. grammar checks, brainstorming, reformatting, short answers, sonnet handles all of this at a fraction of the cost. rule of thumb: if the task takes claude less than 30 seconds to answer, it probably doesn't need opus. switch models before you start the session, it takes 2 clicks.
